paras: The pursuit and shooting at Charles Harris near Leesburg, Georgia, took place in early July 1881, when a member of a citizens' search party chased Harris, a Black railroad worker accused of assaulting a widow, and fired at him with a pistol. Harris returned fire, no one was hit, and he remained at large; the only report found, from the Albany Advertiser, called for his arrest for an "atrocious crime."

Harris belonged to a gang of railroad hands who had been getting out crossties and was said to have come from the neighborhood of Brown's Station. According to the Advertiser, on a Saturday night about 8 o'clock he entered the home of Mrs. P. C. Carroll, a widow living near Leesburg, through a window and struck her with a rock and choked her. She was said to have broken free and fired a shotgun at him twice without effect, after which he stayed a short distance away until morning.

After Mrs. Carroll told her neighbors, her son Will Carroll arrested Harris early the next morning and brought him before her, and she identified him. While Carroll was leading him away, Harris took Carroll's pistol and escaped.

A party was already out looking for Harris, and one of its members, Mr. Fleetwood, chased him on a mule for three miles and then on foot when the mule gave out. Fleetwood fired at Harris with a pistol and Harris fired back, but none of the shots struck anyone.
Harris was still at large when the report was printed, and no report of his recapture, of a trial, or of further violence against him was found.

The story appeared as an Albany Advertiser item reprinted on July 8, 1881, in the Savannah Morning News's "Georgia Affairs" column of state news. The Advertiser gave the accusation as fact, identified Harris throughout as "the negro," and described Mrs. Carroll as "a widow lady of respectability." It reported the shooting without comment and ended by urging that "every effort should be made to arrest the scoundrel."
